justification: None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype linked to ATP2C1 variants. The literature exclusively concerns SPCA1/PMR1 Golgi Ca2+/Mn2+ pump biochemistry, Hailey-Hailey disease (an autosomal dominant skin disorder), cancer, and α-synuclein/Parkinson-related neurodegeneration in yeast models. A small amount of weight is given to "Hypothesized" because calcium homeostasis and secretory-pathway/ER-Golgi stress are broadly relevant mechanisms in neuronal signaling and have been invoked in neurodevelopmental disorders, but no article here makes that link to autism. There are no human genetic studies of ATP2C1 in autism probands or families, so Established and Existing are not supported.

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype; they concern TACC1 in breast/gastric cancer, PI3K inhibitor synergy, family gene structure, and developmental expression patterns (PMIDs 14603251, 12389629, 16496324, 28561737, 24700488, 12087473). There are no human genetic variant studies in autism probands or families, so Established and Existing are unsupported. A small allowance for Hypothesized is warranted because TACC1 is dynamically expressed during embryogenesis (including brain) and functions in centrosome/microtubule and translational-control pathways that are broadly relevant to neurodevelopment, but this is indirect and not framed around autism. On the presented evidence, the gene–phenotype relationship is best described as Novel.

None of the provided articles report any association between ACTN1 variants and Autism Spectrum Disorder. The human genetic evidence for ACTN1 is overwhelmingly for congenital macrothrombocytopenia (PMIDs 23434115, 31237726, 26312134, 41153762), with additional links to cancer, COVID-19 susceptibility, vincristine neuropathy, and myopathy. The only neurodevelopmental co-mention is a multigene 14q24.1q24.3 deletion associated with mild intellectual disability and heart defects (PMID 24357125), which spans 19 genes and cannot implicate ACTN1 specifically, nor does it describe autism. Some weak biological plausibility exists via actin cytoskeletal remodeling, neuromuscular junction formation, and Cullin-3/KBTBD-related pathways (PMID 30990797), since cytoskeletal regulation is broadly relevant to neurodevelopment, justifying a modest Hypothesized allocation. Overall the evidence base is best described as Novel with limited indirect biological plausibility.

Only one human study directly links CEP120 variants to ASD: a small Bulgarian whole-exome cohort (PMID 40558542) reporting novel CEP120 single nucleotide variants in individuals with syndromic/non-syndromic autism, proposed as candidates for diagnostics. This is a single, exploratory candidate-gene report without replication or segregation-based causal proof, so "Established" cannot be supported (no two independent proband/family studies demonstrating causality). Supporting but indirect human evidence comes from CEP120 mutations causing Joubert syndrome (PMIDs 27208211, 38050708, 34711653, 33486889), a ciliopathy with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and developmental delay that is a well-recognized syndromic context for autistic features, strengthening "Existing." The remaining literature is mechanistic (centriole/cilia biology, mouse kidney and cerebellum models, oocyte aneuploidy), which supports a plausible neurodevelopmental biological basis and thus contributes to "Hypothesized" rather than human genetic association. "Novel" is unlikely given the explicit human ASD exome report.

None of the provided articles report autism spectrum disorder in patients with TRAPPC12 variants. The human genetic evidence concerns biallelic TRAPPC12 variants causing progressive encephalopathy with brain atrophy and spasticity (PMID 28777934, 32369837, 36995918) and hydrocephaly (PMID 32347653) — severe neurodevelopmental phenotypes, but not ASD or a recognized ASD subtype. Supportive biological plausibility comes from a mouse/OPC study showing hypomyelination, compromised synaptic function and "aberrant behaviors" with disrupted TRAPPC12–Mea6 trafficking (PMID 38439956), plus roles in ciliogenesis and autophagy (PMID 32258032, 30843302), pathways broadly implicated in neurodevelopment — this is animal/in vitro, so it supports Hypothesized rather than Existing. The Alzheimer neuropathology multivariate GWAS hit (PMID 30683923) spans a contiguous three-gene region and is unrelated to ASD. Hence Hypothesized is most fitting, with meaningful probability that the co-mentions are incidental (Novel).

None of the provided articles reports STAT3 variants in patients with autism spectrum disorder; the STAT3 literature here is overwhelmingly immunological (hyper-IgE syndrome, STAT3 gain-of-function immune dysregulation, LGL leukemia, skeletal development), with neurologic involvement described only rarely and non-specifically (PMIDs 33932191, 36843887, 40880472, 32818584). The two abstracts mentioning ASD do so for other genes: TLK1/TLK2 (PMID 37662408) and PTPRD (PMID 41208653), where STAT3 appears only as a downstream mediator of PTPRD-driven gliogenesis — a tenuous pathway-level co-mention rather than evidence of a STAT3–ASD genetic association. This provides at most a weak biological rationale (JAK-STAT signaling in neurodevelopment/gliogenesis) supporting a "Hypothesized" relationship, and no human genetic data supporting "Existing" or "Established." Because no proband- or family-level ASD variants in STAT3 are cited, "Established" is effectively excluded, and points are split between Novel and Hypothesized.

The strongest human genetic evidence is the Lebanese homozygosity-mapping study (PMID 28358038), which nominated DPP4 as a novel candidate ASD susceptibility gene in consanguineous families — credible but preliminary and unreplicated. A candidate-polymorphism study of DPPIV rs7608798 (PMID 25625371) explicitly found no allele-frequency association with ASD, though it did show genotype-dependent expression differences after β-casomorphin-7 exposure. The 2q24.2q24.3 de novo deletion (PMID 24508274) includes DPP4 but spans 13 genes (including TBR1), so it cannot implicate DPP4 specifically. Substantial biochemical/biomarker work (serum DPPIV levels and activity, opioid-peptide hypothesis; PMIDs 30621149, 26165750, 37294021, 12578238) supports biological plausibility rather than variant-level causation, and results are inconsistent. No two independent studies report causal DPP4 variants in probands/families, so Established is excluded; Existing is most appropriate, with meaningful probability that the evidence is merely mechanistic/hypothesized.

Human genetic evidence exists linking PDE2A to neurodevelopmental phenotypes overlapping ASD: biallelic PDE2A variants cause intellectual disability with paroxysmal dyskinesia/epilepsy (PMIDs 29392776, 32467598, 37317634) and a homozygous splicing mutation was reported in a family with atypical Rett syndrome (PMID 32196122), a phenotype strongly linked to ASD. Additionally, Mendelian randomization work in humans reports a causal relationship between phosphodiesterase 2A and ASD (PMIDs 37605207, 38802917), which is credible but not definitive. However, none of these reports demonstrate ASD itself as the primary diagnosis in two or more independent probands with PDE2A variants; the ASD framing largely comes from rodent models (Pde2a+/- mice, Fmr1-KO rescue by PDE2A inhibition; PMIDs 38154608, 35338117, 30137253), which support only Hypothesized. Therefore Existing is most appropriate, with substantial residual weight on Hypothesized and little support for Established.

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype linked to PAPOLA. The listed papers concern subarachnoid hemorrhage/tumorigenesis transcriptomics (PMID 39726593), postmenopausal osteoporosis co-expression networks (PMID 31432133), reference-gene selection for qPCR normalization (PMID 19584937), translational regulation of PAPOLA mRNA (PMID 20174964), and poly(A) machinery in hibernating ground squirrel adipose tissue (PMID 42201243). There are no human genetic variant studies in autism probands or families, and no functional or animal-model data connecting PAPOLA biology to autism-relevant pathways. Therefore the evidence base is essentially absent, and co-mentions are incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

None of the provided articles mention autism spectrum disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype. All literature concerns MLPH (melanophilin) as a Rab27a/Myosin Va effector in melanosome transport, coat color dilution in cats, dogs, rabbits, mink and quail, Griscelli syndrome type 3 (a pigmentary disorder without neurological involvement), mast cell degranulation, and transcriptional/epigenetic regulation of Mlph expression. Human genetic evidence exists only for hypopigmentation (e.g., MLPH p.R35W in Griscelli syndrome type III), which is not a recognized precursor, subtype, or risk factor for ASD. There is no expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence linking MLPH biology to autism, so co-mentions would be purely incidental.

Both retrieved articles are valproic acid rat models of autism examining hippocampal/prefrontal synaptic and neuroinflammatory changes; neither studies NPEPPS. They were almost certainly retrieved because of the acronym "PSA" (polysialylated form of NCAM), which is a homonym for NPEPPS (puromycin-sensitive aminopeptidase, PSA), and thus must be dismissed. No human genetic variant data, no expression or functional data on NPEPPS, and no mechanistic pathway link to Autism Spectrum Disorder are presented. With only incidental homonym co-mentions and no rodent or in vitro evidence for the actual gene, the relationship is best classified as Novel.

None of the supplied articles mention autism spectrum disorder, autistic traits, or any neurodevelopmental phenotype, and none report CYRIB variants in human probands or families with ASD. The literature provided is centered on CYRI-B (FAM49B) as a RAC1-sequestering negative regulator of the WAVE regulatory complex in cancer metastasis, platelet biology, phagocytosis, and protein structure (PMIDs 38712822, 38391912, 37264948, 33021503); the only human genetic report is a CNV analysis in familial Parkinson's disease (PMID 40037983), which is a different phenotype and a multigene CNV context. The only conceivable link to ASD is indirect biology: CYRI-B acts in the Rac1/CYFIP1/WAVE actin-regulatory pathway, and CYFIP1 is a recognized neurodevelopmental/ASD candidate, which lends modest pathway-level plausibility supporting "Hypothesized." However, since no neuronal, brain-expression, or animal-behavior data for CYRIB are presented here, the co-mentions remain largely incidental, so Novel receives comparable weight, and Established is effectively excluded for lack of any patient variant evidence.

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder, neurodevelopment, or any neuropsychiatric phenotype. The literature set is entirely about NF-YC as a histone-fold subunit of the CCAAT-binding NF-Y transcription factor, covering biochemistry (PMIDs 9153318, 8910521, 9430679), plant biology (33098724, 28526714, 33945672), Drosophila and C. elegans development (18233955, 17216611, 23933492, 17574230), and immune/endocrine regulation (20054001, 34600022). No human genetic variants, probands, or families linked to autism are reported, so Established and Existing are unsupported. Only a very weak, indirect argument for Hypothesized could be made from generic chromatin/transcriptional regulation and developmental roles, which is insufficient to be autism-specific.

Every provided article concerns MTMR2 in the context of Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 4B1 demyelinating neuropathy, myotubularin family phosphoinositide phosphatase biochemistry, myotubular myopathy rescue, or neuronal mitophagy regulation. No article reports autism spectrum disorder phenotypes, ASD cohorts, or ASD-associated variants in MTMR2. The only tenuous biological link is MTMR2's role in neuronal membrane trafficking and autophagy regulation (PMID 40783388), pathways broadly implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, which provides a weak basis for "Hypothesized" but nothing specific to ASD. There are no human genetic studies connecting MTMR2 variants to autism, so Established and Existing are effectively excluded.

None of the provided articles report PPP2R2A variants in individuals with autism spectrum disorder or any neurodevelopmental cohort; the human patient study (PMID 33106617) concerns de novo variants in PPP2R1A, PPP2R5D and PPP2CA, not PPP2R2A, and thus provides only pathway-level (PP2A holoenzyme) plausibility rather than gene-specific evidence. The remaining papers are biochemical/cell-biological studies of PP2A-B55α in mitosis, keratinocyte adhesion, AKT signaling, mitophagy, TGF-β signaling and tau dephosphorylation. Several of these are neurobiologically relevant (tau phosphorylation, AKT/GSK3β signaling, Parkin-dependent mitophagy, neurodegeneration rescue in a fly model), supporting a hypothesized biological link but not a genetic association. No human proband or family data implicating PPP2R2A in ASD is available here, so Established is essentially excluded and Existing is minimally supported only by the analogous PP2A-subunit NDD phenotypes.

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype. The literature on TMC6 concerns epidermodysplasia verruciformis (TMC6-TMC8-CIB1 complex, lymphocyte immunity, βHPV susceptibility) and a sensory role in noxious heat detection in dorsal root ganglion neurons in mice. The DRG/thermosensation work is neuronal but relates to peripheral nociception, not to autism-relevant brain biology, offering only a very tenuous conceptual link (e.g., sensory processing) that is insufficient for a "Hypothesized" designation. No human genetic variants linking TMC6 to ASD are reported in any of these papers, so "Established" and "Existing" are not supported.

The strongest human genetic datum is the NDD burden re-analysis (PMID 38965372), which identified a qualifying ultra-rare de novo variant in VCP among candidate genes in an unsolved neurodevelopmental disorder cohort, but VCP was not further validated with additional probands and the paper's own conclusions focused on LEO1 and PCBP2. Reviews (PMIDs 29310658, 26819769) assert VCP mutations are involved in ASD and describe VCP's role in dendritic spinogenesis and ER formation/protein synthesis, but these are background citations plus mechanistic/cell-biology data rather than primary patient-variant evidence. The remaining literature concerns VCP multisystem proteinopathy, IBMPFD, FTD, myopathy and vacuolar tauopathy, which are unrelated adult phenotypes. Thus there is limited but credible human evidence plus strong biological plausibility, favoring "Existing" with substantial weight on "Hypothesized"; there are no two independent proband/family reports establishing causality for ASD.

None of the provided articles mention autism spectrum disorder at all. The TPCN1 genetic evidence presented concerns non-Alzheimer's dementias (a structural deletion associated with Lewy body dementia) and LATE-NC/Alzheimer's-related neuropathology, which are late-onset neurodegenerative phenotypes, not ASD precursors or subtypes. The remaining literature is mechanistic work on two-pore channel endolysosomal Ca2+/Na+ signaling, NAADP, autophagy, viral entry, and lysosomal storage disease models—biology that is broadly neuronally relevant but with no articulated link to autism. At most, one could argue a weak hypothesized link via lysosomal Ca2+ signaling and neurodevelopmental/synaptic trafficking, but this is speculative and not stated in any abstract. No human ASD probands, families, or association studies are reported, so Established and Existing are effectively excluded.

No article reports pathogenic EPS8 variants in autism probands or families; the only human EPS8 variant evidence concerns autosomal recessive deafness (DFNB102, PMIDs 24741995, 36635257), a distinct phenotype. The autism link rests on mouse work showing Eps8-null animals have immature dendritic spines, impaired LTP, altered NMDA receptor GluN2A/GluN2B composition, and cognitive deficits (PMIDs 23685357, 30233314), plus a human observation of reduced EPS8 protein levels in postmortem brains of ASD patients — expression, not genetic variation, which per the rules supports "Hypothesized." That patient-derived protein finding is a genuine human association, so a modest allocation to "Existing" is warranted, but it is a single unreplicated expression study rather than variant-level evidence. Established is essentially excluded because no two independent studies report EPS8 variants causing ASD.

None of the provided articles reports human genetic variants in MLLT10 (AF10) in autism probands or families, so Established is not supportable; no PMID here demonstrates a causal or even associative link with ASD. The literature supplied is centered on leukemia biology (MLL fusion partners, DOT1L-mediated H3K79 methylation, transcriptional elongation) and Wnt/TCF4–β-catenin signaling in intestinal homeostasis (PMID 21103407), none of which addresses ASD phenotypes. The only neurodevelopmental relevance is indirect: the Drosophila AF10/AF17 homolog Dalf is required in the nervous system for maintaining EVE expression and normal growth (PMID 11165485), and the AF4/AF10/AF9/DOT1L complex paper (PMID 17135274) invokes cerebellar Purkinje cell function and FRAXE/FMR2 intellectual disability. These give a thin, non-specific biological rationale (chromatin regulation in neurons) that could support a weak Hypothesized rating, but they are in flies/in vitro and not tied to autism. Accordingly, most weight falls on Novel with a substantial minority on Hypothesized.

The strongest mechanistic evidence is functional: Mcf2l binds the cytoplasmic TIR domain of IL1RAPL1, an X-linked intellectual disability/autism gene, and mediates excitatory synapse formation and AMPA receptor trafficking via RhoA-ROCK signaling (PMID 23785489) — but this work is in cultured cortical neurons, not human genetic variation, so it supports "Hypothesized." The only human report is a single child with a ring chromosome 13 and a 2.11-Mb 13q34 deletion spanning 23 genes, where MCF2L was speculatively implicated (PMID 25171325); a multigene CNV in one proband cannot single out MCF2L and does not constitute replicated causal evidence. The West Nile virus study (PMID 33302579) involves MCF2L but an unrelated phenotype and reports no statistically significant loci. No article reports MCF2L point variants in independent autism probands or families, so "Established" is essentially excluded, and only modest weight goes to "Existing" based on the suggestive deletion case plus the direct pathway link to a known ASD gene.

The only direct human evidence linking EXT2 sequence variants to autism is a single case report of a patient with compound heterozygous likely pathogenic EXT2 variants presenting with developmental delay, autism, epilepsy, and macrocephaly (PMID 30997052) — one proband, insufficient for "Established". Other autism-related reports either implicate EXT1 rather than EXT2 (PMID 12032595) or involve contiguous 11p11.2 deletions (Potocki-Shaffer syndrome) where autism is attributed to PHF21A haploinsufficiency, and multigene deletions cannot single out EXT2 (PMIDs 30487643, 36555772). The remaining literature concerns EXT2's role in heparan sulfate biosynthesis and hereditary multiple exostoses/osteochondroma, which provides a plausible neurodevelopmental mechanism (HS signaling in brain) but no direct autism variant evidence (PMIDs 29277722, 36402845). Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing" (one credible human report), with meaningful residual probability for "Hypothesized" if the single case is considered too weak.

Only one article in this set connects KIF5A to autism: the large NDD CNV resource (PMID 31602316), which lists KIF5A among genes recurrently impacted by rare CNVs across ASD, ADHD, SCZ and OCD cohorts. This is human genetic data but the evidence is limited and derives from multi-gene copy number events that cannot isolate KIF5A from neighbouring genes, so it cannot support "Established" and only weakly supports "Existing". All remaining papers concern KIF5A in ALS, hereditary spastic paraplegia, CMT2, and optic neuropathy (PMIDs 29342275, 15452312, 33829936, 32888732, 38499745), with neurodevelopmental relevance limited to neonatal intractable myoclonus (PMID 40524150) — a neurodevelopmental but not autism phenotype, which lends some biological plausibility (Hypothesized). No independent probands or families with KIF5A point variants and ASD are reported anywhere in this list, so Established is essentially excluded, and a meaningful share of probability remains for Novel given the purely incidental co-mention.

No article reports pathogenic OPA1 sequence variants causing ASD in independent probands; OPA1 variants are established for dominant optic atrophy/neuro-ophthalmic syndromes (PMIDs 19389487, 29454676, 36813316), not autism. The only ASD-linked genetic finding is a multigene 3q29 deletion encompassing 10 genes including OPA1 (PMID 26620927), where the authors themselves attribute the neuropsychiatric phenotype to ATP13A4/HES1 and OPA1 only to optic atrophy — a CNV cannot single out OPA1. Human evidence supporting a biological link includes decreased OPA1 fusion protein in postmortem ASD temporal cortex (PMID 23333625), differential OPA1 promoter methylation in an ASD cohort (PMID 34381777), and altered OPA1 expression in ASD oral mucosa (PMID 31018497); these are expression/epigenetic correlates rather than causal variants, supporting a mechanistic (mitochondrial dynamics) hypothesis. Remaining support comes from in vitro (PPA-treated SH-SY5Y, PMID 37582965) and mouse Foxp1+/- models (PMIDs 35165191, 35052467), which are non-human/functional and thus reinforce "Hypothesized," with partial weight to "Existing" for the human association data.

None of the provided articles reports any genetic association between KTN1 variants and Autism Spectrum Disorder; the only paper mentioning autism (PMID 23406908) concerns thalamic lesions and prefrontal dendrites and does not involve KTN1. Human genetic evidence for KTN1 exists, but for other phenotypes: putamen/subcortical volumes (PMID 25607358), ADHD (PMIDs 32190980, 36609385, 32956741), substance dependence (PMID 32115811), and schizophrenia (PMID 39148597). Several papers use "KTN1" as the Arabidopsis katanin gene, an unrelated homonymous usage that should be dismissed. The neurodevelopmental/brain-volume regulatory biology and ADHD associations provide a weak, indirect biological rationale that could support a "Hypothesized" relationship, but ADHD is not a recognized precursor or subtype of ASD, so direct evidence remains absent, leaving Novel nearly equally plausible.

The strongest human evidence is a single case report of homozygosity for a proven KIT mutation causing piebaldism together with deafness, developmental delay and autism spectrum disorder (PMID 23399981), plus an extended-family exome sequencing study of autism that reports candidate genes shared across neurodevelopmental disorders (PMID 24410847). This is at most one clear proband with a KIT variant and an untargeted sequencing report, which is insufficient for replication across independent probands/families required for "Established". Other listed articles concern KIT signal transduction, cardiac fibroblasts, mast cell mediator disorders and c-Kit+ cell transplantation hypotheses (PMIDs 10909038, 9338533, 35841449, 30884251, 21225454), which provide only biological/hypothetical or non-human support, and one paper (GCPII polymorphism, PMID 22310383) mentions "kit" only as a laboratory assay homonym. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing", with meaningful residual probability for "Hypothesized" if the single case is judged coincidental or attributable to the broader syndrome.

No article reports pathogenic VLDLR variants causing autism in patients; the human VLDLR variant literature (PMIDs 18326629, 27000652, 39085459, 23670308, 20199520) concerns CAMRQ1/VLDLR cerebellar hypoplasia with ataxia and intellectual disability, not ASD, so the "Established" bar (two independent variant-based studies in ASD probands) is not met. The candidate-gene association studies that directly tested VLDLR in autism cohorts were negative for VLDLR itself, with signals falling on RELN/DAB1 (PMIDs 26285919, 23333377); the language-cluster analysis (PMID 36039581) is the only possible weak human genetic signal and is not clearly positive for VLDLR. Human post-mortem data showing elevated VLDLR mRNA in autistic brain (PMID 15820235) is expression, not variant, evidence, and the supportive functional work is in mice and zebrafish (PMIDs 27184477, 23110844, 31607872), with the zebrafish vldlr mutant actually failing to show social deficits. The strong pathway rationale (Reelin–VLDLR/ApoER2–Dab1 signaling reviewed in PMIDs 31022460, 32604886) makes "Hypothesized" the best fit, with residual probability for "Existing" given the human expression finding and possible subtype association.

The strongest evidence is PMID 40475134, which reports eight unrelated individuals with de novo/heterozygous ABI2 missense variants (including a recurrent SH3-domain p.Tyr491Cys) presenting with intellectual disability, epilepsy, brain malformations and explicitly "autistic traits" — direct human variant-level evidence, but from a single report and with autism as a secondary feature rather than a primary diagnosis. PMID 28397838 adds human loss-of-function ABI2 variants in consanguineous families with autosomal recessive intellectual disability, a neurodevelopmental phenotype strongly linked to ASD, supporting but not replicating the ASD-specific association. Counterbalancing this, the only dedicated autism study (PMID 15542242) tested ABI2 as a positional candidate in the chromosome 2q linkage region and found no allelic association. Remaining papers concern ABI2's cytoskeletal/WAVE-complex and oncologic biology (PMIDs 37042842, 40668190, 11387320, 18161990), which provide mechanistic plausibility for neurodevelopment but not ASD-specific genetic evidence. Because I cannot cite two independent clinical studies establishing ABI2 variants as a cause of ASD, "Established" is not warranted, and points concentrate on "Existing."

Only one article in the list connects TJP2 to autism: an integrative human genomic analysis of ASD GWAS data with m6A/m5C variant annotation, cis-eQTL and differential expression, which flags rs3812536 near TJP2 as a candidate causal variant (PMID 39738578). This is a single in silico/human-data study without independent replication or patient-level variant validation, so it cannot support "Established"; no paper reports TJP2 variants in ASD probands or families. All remaining articles concern TJP2 in progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 4, hepatocellular carcinoma, retinal pigment epithelium barrier function, and tight-junction biology, with no relevance to neurodevelopment or autism. Points are therefore concentrated on "Existing" (one credible but limited human association), with substantial weight on "Hypothesized"/"Novel" because the single finding is purely computational and the tight-junction biology link to ASD is not directly demonstrated here.

No article in this set reports AGAP3 variants identified in autism probands or families; there is therefore no basis for Established, and no human genetic association study specific to ASD supports Existing. The available evidence is biological/mechanistic: AGAP3 (centaurin-γ3/CRAG) is a SynGAP-interacting postsynaptic GTPase enriched in the developing brain, and forebrain-specific Crag/Agap3 knockout mice show an immature dentate gyrus and hyperactivity, a phenotype shared with neuropsychiatric/neurodevelopmental disorder models (PMID 33811862, 31882856, 21832068). The SRRM2 study (PMID 42189682) links AGAP3 mis-splicing to schizophrenia/neurodevelopmental disorder mechanisms, but the causal variants are in SRRM2, not AGAP3, and the human iPSC data only show splicing changes downstream of SRRM2 loss. The Alzheimer's biomarker paper (PMID 36110430) is expression-based and phenotype-irrelevant to ASD. Overall this fits Hypothesized, with residual probability on Novel given ASD itself is only indirectly implicated.

The only provided article is a mouse QTL study linking a Chromosome 7 interval containing Syt9 and Ppfibp2 to locomotor and rearing responses after morphine treatment (PMID 27746909). This is an animal behavioral pharmacology study with no measurement of autism-related phenotypes and no human genetic data, so it cannot support Established or Existing categories. The only tenuous link is that PPFIBP2 is a liprin-family gene with plausible synaptic/neural relevance, but nothing in the provided literature connects it mechanistically or genetically to Autism Spectrum Disorder. Therefore the co-mention is essentially incidental, and the relationship is best described as Novel, with a small allowance for a Hypothesized reading based on the gene's neural/behavioral candidacy.

No article reports STAT1 variants in autism probands or families; the vast majority of the corpus concerns STAT1 gain-of-function immunodeficiency (chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, autoimmunity, infections), which is unrelated to ASD (PMIDs 32852681, 27114460, 37406138, 30280610). Only two papers touch autism: a single-cell phospho-flow study that included ASC patients and measured Stat1 (pY701), but the STAT1-related network alteration was found in bipolar/major depressive disorder rather than ASC (PMID 30038233), and a bioinformatic study of MER41 LTR/STAT1 binding sites that explicitly found no significant enrichment in ASD-associated gene promoters (PMID 31031802). Thus there is a weak biological/pathway rationale (immune-IFN-γ/STAT1 signaling in neurodevelopment and behavior) but no human genetic association, supporting Hypothesized, with substantial probability that the co-mentions are essentially incidental (Novel). Established is effectively excluded since no PMID demonstrates causal STAT1 variants in autism patients.

None of the provided articles report ACTN2 variants in autism spectrum disorder patients or any ASD-related cohort; the human genetic literature here is exclusively about cardiomyopathies (HCM, DCM, LVNC, RCM) and distal/congenital myopathies (PMIDs 36116040, 30900782, 34170073, 33859969). The only neurobiological links are indirect: alpha-actinin-2 anchors NMDA receptors together with PSD-95 in brain (PMID 14678777) and one review vaguely mentions neurodegenerative conditions (PMID 42111349), which provides a synaptic-scaffold rationale but no ASD-specific data, and the NMDA receptor work was performed in transgenic Huntington's mice. A multigene 1q43 deletion case (PMID 37374362) involves cardiac phenotypes only and cannot implicate ACTN2 in ASD. Therefore Established and Existing are not supportable; the evidence sits between Novel and a weak Hypothesized link through synaptic scaffolding biology.

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder, autistic traits, or any neurodevelopmental phenotype in relation to DPP9. The literature set concerns DPP9's role in NLRP1/CARD8 inflammasome regulation, COVID-19 severity GWAS, kidney injury/ferroptosis, ovarian carcinoma, and a Mendelian immunodeficiency (Hatipoglu syndrome) characterized by cytopenias, infections, and failure to thrive — not autism. No human genetic study links DPP9 variants to ASD, so Established and Existing are unsupported. A minimal Hypothesized weight is retained only because DPP9 belongs to the DPPIV gene family that includes DPP6 and DPP10 (neuronal genes with reported neurodevelopmental associations) and because inflammasome/IL-1β signaling has been broadly invoked in neuroinflammation, but this is indirect and speculative rather than DPP9-specific.

The strongest link is a mouse model: conditional APP/APLP1/APLP2 triple knockout in forebrain excitatory neurons produces an autism-like phenotype with repetitive behaviors, impaired social communication and social interaction deficits (PMID 34008862), which is animal evidence and therefore supports "Hypothesized" rather than "Existing". Additional mechanistic work shows APP/APLP2 regulate synaptic transmission, glutamatergic signaling, spine density and NMDAR/calcineurin regulation (PMIDs 26551565, 18535156, 39732167, 41187812), all biologically plausible pathways for neurodevelopmental/ASD phenotypes but derived from cell and mouse systems. The only human genetic report is a family-based WES study of specific language impairment where rare co-segregating APLP2 variants were found, but the statistically significant and highlighted gene was BUD13, and SLI is a related but distinct neurodevelopmental phenotype (PMID 35053791); this gives some weak support for "Existing". No study reports ASD-causing APLP2 variants in independent human probands or families, so "Established" is essentially excluded.

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder or any autism-related neurodevelopmental phenotype. The human genetic evidence for NNT concerns familial glucocorticoid deficiency/primary adrenal insufficiency (PMIDs 27129361, 38261461, 37352919, 35627102, 36478070), plus unrelated associations with migraine, hearing loss, sebaceous hyperplasia, and cardiac phenotypes. The only conceivable indirect link is NNT's role in mitochondrial redox homeostasis and oxidative stress, a general mechanism sometimes discussed in ASD, but no article here makes that connection, so it remains speculative rather than literature-supported. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a modest allowance for a mechanistic (Hypothesized) argument via mitochondrial dysfunction.

None of the provided articles mention autism spectrum disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype linked to NFATC4 variants; there are no human genetic association or proband/family studies at all. The bulk of the literature concerns cardiac hypertrophy, adipocyte/metabolic signaling, muscle fiber typing, osteoclasts, and endurance athlete phenotypes, which are irrelevant to ASD. The only tangentially supportive material is neuronal: NFATC4 mRNA expression in mouse and human brain and activity/calcineurin-dependent nuclear translocation of NFAT isoforms in cortical and hippocampal neurons regulating genes involved in axon growth, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal survival (PMIDs 18675896, 26851544), plus glial/myelination and lysosomal Ca2+ roles (PMIDs 33879538, 35150145, 41512030). This provides only a generic calcium/calcineurin-signaling rationale, insufficient to establish a directed ASD hypothesis, so the weight rests on Novel with a substantial minority for Hypothesized.

None of the provided articles mention autism spectrum disorder, autistic features, or any neurodevelopmental/behavioral phenotype. CEP78 evidence is confined to cone-rod dystrophy, Usher-like syndrome with hearing loss, retinitis pigmentosa, male infertility/MMAF/OAT, CAKUT, and centriolar/ciliogenesis cell biology (PMIDs 27627988, 35240912, 38780195, 36756949, 36206347, 39747485, 34259627, 40777246, 42265085). The only tenuous conceptual link is that CEP78 is a ciliary/centrosomal protein and primary cilia signaling has broad relevance to neurodevelopment, which grants a small amount of weight to "Hypothesized," but no CNS or behavioral data are presented. There are no human genetic studies connecting CEP78 variants to ASD, so "Established" and "Existing" are essentially excluded.

All ALDH3A2 articles concern Sjögren-Larsson syndrome (ichthyosis, spasticity, intellectual disability, leukoencephalopathy) and none report autism or autistic features as a phenotype in patients with ALDH3A2 variants (PMIDs 32021380, 30372562, 28543186, 15931689, 11306053). The only two abstracts mentioning autism involve entirely different genes (SCLT1 in PMID 30425282; CEP290/AHI1 in PMID 20683928) and are incidental co-mentions rather than ALDH3A2 evidence. No human genetic study here links ALDH3A2 variants to Autism Spectrum Disorder, so Established and Existing are not supportable. A modest allowance for "Hypothesized" is given because ALDH3A2 deficiency causes a neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability and white matter disease, a biologically plausible (though unproven) route to autistic features.

None of the retrieved autism-related articles concern PSMD1; they were captured through the homonym "S1" (primary somatosensory cortex, sleep stage 1) and involve unrelated genes (FMR1, SHANK3, CNTNAP2, NRP1). The genuine PSMD1 papers address proteasome biology/SUMOylation (PMID 24910440), arsenic exposure (PMID 31965495), obesity epigenetics (PMID 29762635), thyroid ophthalmopathy, myelodysplastic syndrome, and alpha-synuclein degradation (PMID 30745870) — none report autism phenotypes or ASD-associated variants. The only tenuous conceptual bridge is the evolutionary/genomic linkage of Psmd1 with the serotonin receptor gene Htr2b (PMID 30223085) and a finasteride nucleus accumbens proteomic change (PMID 27750143), which offer only very indirect neurobiological relevance. There is no human genetic association, so Established and Existing are not supportable; a small allowance is given to Hypothesized based on proteasome/UPS involvement in neurodevelopment and the serotonergic linkage.

Biallelic SNX14 variants are firmly established as causing SCAR20, a neurodevelopmental syndrome with intellectual disability, ataxia and coarse facies, but autism is only intermittently reported as part of that phenotype rather than being the primary studied outcome. PMID 37485342 explicitly lists autism among the defining SCAR20 features while reporting a novel deep intronic variant in two affected sisters, and PMID 33193593 documents stereotypies (an autism-related behavioral feature) in siblings with compound heterozygous SNX14 variants; other patient reports (25439728, 25848753, 30473892, 27913285, 41294032) describe ID/ataxia without formal ASD diagnoses. Thus human variant-level evidence connecting SNX14 to autistic features exists but is limited, largely descriptive, and not replicated with rigorous ASD phenotyping, falling short of "Established." Supporting mechanistic plausibility comes from neuronal Snx14 function in excitability and synaptic transmission in mice (24859318) and autophagy/lipid pathway roles (25848753, 29635513), which underpins the "Hypothesized" allocation.

The strongest human evidence is a transcriptome-wide association study integrating ASD GWAS summary data with mRNA expression profiles, which nominated MED15 as one of five overlapping candidate genes (PMID 30561910); this is a single, nominally significant (P ≈ 0.03) association, so it supports "Existing" but is far from definitive. MED15 also lies within the 22q11.2 region implicated in neurodevelopmental phenotypes including ASD (PMIDs 30614210, 23791650), but these are multigene CNVs that cannot isolate MED15 from neighboring genes and therefore do not constitute gene-level causal evidence. Remaining literature is mechanistic or non-ASD: MED15 in senescence and cognitive decline in mice (PMID 40825935), Huntington's disease modifier interactions (PMIDs 39763784, 40501897, 40169779), yeast/C. elegans transcriptional biology, and cancer—supporting plausible neurobiological relevance ("Hypothesized") rather than variant-level ASD causation. No article reports MED15 point variants in independent ASD probands or families, so "Established" is essentially excluded.

A single human candidate-gene association study directly reports that BAIAP2 variation is associated with autism (PMID 20888579), which meets the bar for "Existing" but is not replicated by independent proband/family studies in this set. Other human variant studies implicate de novo BAIAP2 missense variants in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (PMID 41133935) and lissencephaly (PMID 38149472), and association with ADHD (PMID 24377651) — related neurodevelopmental phenotypes that support, but do not establish, an ASD-specific causal role. The bulk of the ASD-relevant evidence is from IRSp53/Baiap2 knockout mouse models showing social deficits and NMDAR dysfunction (PMIDs 25622145, 35982261, 36317872, 32116566), which is functional/animal evidence supporting "Hypothesized" rather than human causality. No two human studies here report independent ASD probands with single-gene BAIAP2 variants, so "Established" is not warranted.

All DDX11-specific clinical papers (PMIDs 20137776, 30216658, 28960803, 30924321, 25701697, 36703504, 40937658, 42107920) describe Warsaw breakage syndrome — growth restriction, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and sensorineural hearing loss — with no report of autism spectrum disorder in any proband. The remaining DDX11 papers are mechanistic/oncologic (cohesion, autophagy, HCC) and make no ASD link. The two articles that do mention autism (PMIDs 31182634, 28839197) concern CHL1 (Close Homolog of L1), a distinct neural adhesion molecule that only shares the "Chl1/ChlR1" acronym with DDX11, and are therefore homonym artifacts to be dismissed. At best, one can hypothesize a link via the broader neurodevelopmental/cohesinopathy phenotype (intellectual disability, chromatin-loop regulation of neurodevelopmental gene expression), but this is indirect and unmeasured for ASD, so the evidence base is essentially novel with a modest hypothesized component.

The bulk of the evidence linking OPRM1 to ASD comes from the Oprm1 knockout mouse, which is explicitly proposed as a monogenic mouse model recapitulating core autistic-like behaviors, with oxytocin, mGluR4, bromide and behavioral-intervention rescue studies (PMIDs 24619243, 39020142, 35418620, 30242222, 27274875, 25225634), plus Oprm1 as a downstream mediator of social deficits in the MECP2 duplication mouse (PMID 22231481) — all animal work, which supports Hypothesized. Human data are limited: altered OPRM1 mRNA expression in blood of children with ASD (PMID 30519864) is expression, not variant, evidence; the single human genotyping study of A118G explicitly found no association between OPRM1 alleles and ASD incidence, reporting only genotype-dependent expression responses to β-casomorphin-7 (PMID 25625371). Other human-focused papers (opioid receptor pharmacogenetics, neuropathic pain, resilience, lateral septum transcriptomics) concern non-ASD phenotypes. No article reports causal OPRM1 variants in independent ASD probands or families, so Established is effectively excluded; Existing retains modest weight because of the human expression and pharmacogenetic-expression findings.

None of the provided articles report TFG variants in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder; the human genetic literature exclusively links TFG to hereditary spastic paraplegia, HMSN-P, Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2, infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, ALS/α-synucleinopathy and multisystem proteinopathy (PMIDs 37890998, 25098539, 29971521, 38837630, 34779525). Therefore neither Established nor Existing can be supported, since no proband or family with ASD is described. A weak biological rationale exists: TFG regulates ER-to-Golgi secretory transport and Rab4A-positive recycling endosome trafficking in neurons, with downregulated inhibitory receptor signaling suggested to cause excitation–inhibition imbalance (PMID 36161950), and it proteolytically interacts with synaptic proteins such as DLGAP4, IQSEC1 and MPDZ (PMID 40650235) — pathways broadly relevant to neurodevelopmental disorders. However, these data come from rat/CRISPR-edited neurons and cell lines and address neurodegeneration rather than autism, so the majority of probability rests on Novel with a substantial minority on Hypothesized.

None of the provided articles examine autism spectrum disorder, and no human genetic study reports MIB2 variants in autistic probands or families, so Established and Existing are effectively unsupported. Human variant reports for MIB2 concern left ventricular non-compaction/Ménétrier-like gastropathy (PMID 28013292), bicuspid aortic valve (PMID 36071494) and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy expression (PMID 41272943), none of which are ASD precursors or subtypes. The only tenuous neurobiological link is the mention of postulated Notch-independent roles of Mib2 in NMDA receptor activity, which was explicitly not confirmed in zebrafish mutants (PMID 26519518), plus generic Notch-pathway involvement (PMIDs 17196985, 25565632) and a neural tube closure defect in Mib2-null mice (PMID 17987667) — animal/in vitro data that could at best support a weak hypothesis. Overall the evidence base is dominated by inflammation, ubiquitination, muscle and cancer biology, with autism only incidental, favoring Novel.

No article reports POLG variants segregating with or causing Autism Spectrum Disorder in patients. The bulk of the POLG literature here (PMIDs 30451971, 20301791, 18546365, 21880868, 16177225, 40811876, 38294884) describes POLG-related mitochondrial disease phenotypes (Alpers-Huttenlocher, MEMSA, PEO, neuropathy, epilepsy), which are not ASD. The one directly ASD-focused study of POLG (PMID 39611328) examined mtDNA replisome gene expression in oral mucosa of children with ASD and found no significant difference in POLG expression, i.e., a negative human result, though it establishes a plausible mitochondrial/mtDNA-maintenance pathway link. In the clinical vignette (PMID 34840252) POLG sequencing was performed in an autistic child and was normal, with the causal variant found in STXBP1 — a co-mention, not evidence. The DDR/mitochondrial ultrarare variant study in PANS/autism regression (PMID 41662332) raises a speculative possibility but does not specify POLG findings, so the biology-based "Hypothesized" category is most appropriate, with some residual weight on "Novel."

The only article linking CD44 to autism is the TBR1 review/analysis (PMID 25600067), which identifies Cd44 as a downstream transcriptional target of the ASD-causative transcription factor TBR1 and groups it with membrane adhesion proteins regulating neuronal migration and axonal outgrowth; the experimental validation is in Tbr1-deficient mice, not human probands. That paper's mention of prior ASD association is background citation rather than primary genetic evidence, and no article here reports CD44 variants in patients with ASD. All remaining CD44 articles concern cancer, angiogenesis, renal fibrosis, infection, vascular ageing, or retinal Müller cell biology, with no autism relevance, while the other ASD papers (SHANK3, CHD8, NLGN3, BDNF) do not implicate CD44. This pattern—plausible neurodevelopmental biology and a pathway/animal-model link but no human genetic evidence—fits "Hypothesized," with some residual probability of an unlisted human association study or of the co-mention being incidental.

No articles were provided linking C6ORF58 to Autism Spectrum Disorder. C6ORF58 (LEG1 homolog) encodes a secreted salivary/liver-enriched glycoprotein with no established neurodevelopmental function or reported pathogenic variants in ASD probands. Without any literature evidence—genetic, expression, pathway, or animal model—the relationship must be considered novel. A small residual probability is retained for uncited evidence, such as incidental inclusion in exome or CNV studies.

None of the provided articles reports variants in CGGBP1 in autistic probands or families, nor any case-control/association study for Autism Spectrum Disorder, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The biological relevance comes indirectly through CGGBP1's specific binding to unmethylated CGG repeats in the FMR1 5'UTR and modulation of the FMR1 promoter (PMIDs 9201980, 10692448, 20141036), and fragile X syndrome is the most common monogenic cause of ASD, giving a plausible mechanistic/pathway link. However, one study explicitly found that CGGBP1 knockdown does not affect FMR1 transcription or CGG repeat stability (PMID 26306647), weakening the mechanistic case. The remaining papers concern methylation, genome evolution, cell cycle, and cancer, with no autism relevance, so a substantial share remains for Novel while Hypothesized is the best fit.

No article here reports pathogenic DNM1L variants in patients diagnosed with ASD; the clinical DNM1L literature (PMIDs 26825290, 27328748, 35914810, 38341530, 39063023, 38481935, 41008537) describes encephalopathy, epilepsy, optic atrophy, hypotonia and cardiomyopathy, so the Established bar (two independent probands/families with ASD) is not met. The strongest human ASD-linked evidence is expression/association work: Anitha et al. (PMID 23116158) performed brain expression plus genetic association analyses of mitochondrial fission/fusion genes including DNM1L in autism, and postmortem ASD temporal cortex shows elevated Drp1 protein (PMID 23333625), with altered DRP1 transcript in oral mucosa of ASD children (PMID 31018497). These are human but largely expression-level and, at best, a limited/unreplicated association, so Existing is plausible but not secure. Remaining support (butyrate LCL work PMID 29391397, Foxp1 mouse models PMIDs 35165191, 35052467, BDE-209 rat model) is mechanistic/animal, supporting Hypothesized as the most probable category.

Multiple human studies report CACNA1H variants in ASD probands: Splawski et al. found missense variants in 6/461 ASD cases with functional reduction of Cav3.2 currents (PMID 16754686), a Brazilian trio cohort reported a de novo loss-of-function variant in an ASD proband (PMID 31696658), biallelic rare damaging missense variants were found in two ASD families with supporting electrophysiology (PMID 35350424), and a de novo splicing variant was characterized in an oligogenic ASD case with RELN (PMID 35668055). However, these same studies explicitly state that the variants do not segregate with phenotype, exert only mild functional effects, or act only as contributory/oligogenic risk factors, and CACNA1H's monogenic status has been disputed in the related epilepsy literature (PMID 32227660). Thus the human evidence is real and repeated but establishes susceptibility rather than definitive causation, best fitting "Existing" with a residual chance of "Established."

None of the provided articles report DCLK3 variants in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder, nor any autism cohort, case, or family study; ASD is not even mentioned. The strongest relevant material is biological: DCLK3 is a neuron-enriched kinase, and constitutive/conditional Dclk3 knockout mice show anxiety-like behaviour, spatial memory deficits, altered GABAA receptor subunit expression, downregulated immediate early genes, and chromatin/transcriptional regulation changes (PMID 39908340, 29534157) — mechanisms broadly relevant to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric phenotypes, but these are murine/in vitro data. The kinase-biology and substrate paper (PMID 40902973) and the proteomics tissue-expression paper (PMID 30272454) provide only general neurobiological/expression context. The passing statement that "Dclk3 variants are risk factors for psychiatric disorders" is background citation rather than autism-specific evidence, so "Existing" cannot be supported; the evidence best fits "Hypothesized," with meaningful probability that the link is entirely incidental (Novel).

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype. The DDX28/MDDX28 literature here concerns mitochondrial/nuclear localization of a putative DEAD-box RNA helicase in COS-1 cells and rat liver, and an eQTL analysis linking a colorectal cancer risk variant to DDX28 expression in colon tissue. There are no patient variants, no autism cohorts, and no functional or pathway link to autism biology. Consequently the gene–phenotype relationship is best classified as Novel, with only a small residual allowance for a generic mitochondrial-dysfunction rationale that is not actually articulated in these papers.

No study in this set reports CLASP1 variants in autism probands or families, so Established is excluded. The strongest link is functional: CHyMErA-seq microexon perturbation showed that the Clasp1 microexon is required for correct temporal expression of autism-linked genes during neurogenesis (PMID 41633977), which is a pathway/mechanistic argument rather than human genetic association. A consanguineous family with biallelic CLASP1 variants implicates the gene in lissencephaly/neuronal migration defects (PMID 39040917), a human neurodevelopmental phenotype that is related to but not a recognized ASD subtype or precursor, which gives modest weight to Existing. The remaining papers concern CLASP1's microtubule/kinetochore cell-biology functions or unrelated homonym contexts (mitosis, Theileria, ACE-inhibitor cough GWAS) and do not bear on ASD. Overall, the evidence best fits Hypothesized.

The only available article (PMID 31949211) is a mouse study of Fam151b, the paralogue of FAM151A, showing retinal degeneration; Fam151a-null mice explicitly had no discernible phenotype and no neurodevelopmental or autism-like assessment was reported. There are no human genetic studies linking FAM151A variants to Autism Spectrum Disorder, so Established and Existing are effectively excluded. A tenuous biological argument could be made because the C. elegans menorin homologue is involved in neuronal branching, which gives a slim basis for a Hypothesized relationship. However, given the absence of any autism-relevant phenotype or pathway data, Novel is the most appropriate classification.

No human genetic study in this set links FABP1 variants to Autism Spectrum Disorder; the human variant literature (T94A, rs2241883, rs1545224) concerns dyslipidemia, NAFLD, cholesterol uptake, and hepatocellular adenoma, not neurodevelopmental phenotypes (PMIDs 25732850, 24875102, 22465531, 34418801, 27117865). The only ASD-relevant article is a zebrafish valproic acid model in which fabp1 appears merely as one of several downregulated PPAR-pathway transcripts, rescued by rosiglitazone (PMID 41354618) — animal/expression data at best, and FABP1 is not the focus. This provides a thin pathway/expression rationale supporting at most "Hypothesized," with a comparable chance that the co-mention is entirely incidental ("Novel"). Established is excluded outright, as no article reports FABP1 variants in autism probands or families.

No articles were provided linking FAM81B to Autism Spectrum Disorder, so there is no evidence of any kind—genetic, functional, or biological—supporting a relationship. FAM81B is a poorly characterized family-with-sequence-similarity gene with no established neurodevelopmental role in the supplied literature. Without any human variant reports in probands or families, categories of Established and Existing cannot be supported. A small residual probability is retained for Hypothesized in case unlisted expression or pathway data exist, but the evidence base here points to Novel.

No articles were provided, so there is no literature evidence linking H4C7 (histone H4 cluster member 7) to Autism Spectrum Disorder. H4C7 is one of many nearly identical replication-dependent histone H4 genes in the histone cluster, and no variant-level, expression, or functional data supporting a role in ASD is available here. Chromatin/histone biology is broadly relevant to neurodevelopmental disorders, which leaves a small allowance for a hypothesized relationship, but nothing gene-specific is documented. Without any cited studies in human probands, Established and Existing cannot be supported.

No articles were provided linking FKBP1C to Autism Spectrum Disorder or to any relevant neurodevelopmental biology. FKBP1C is a poorly characterized FKBP family member (often annotated as a pseudogene-like paralog) with no reported disease-associated variants in the supplied literature. Without any human genetic evidence, functional data, or even pathway-level co-mention, no case can be made for Established, Existing, or Hypothesized. The relationship is therefore best classified as Novel.

No articles were provided linking GOLGA6C to Autism Spectrum Disorder. GOLGA6C is a member of the golgin A6 family located in a segmentally duplicated, highly repetitive region of chromosome 15, which is difficult to assay reliably and rarely implicated in disease. Without any supporting literature demonstrating variants in patients or relevant functional/biological evidence, there is no basis for an Established, Existing, or Hypothesized designation. The evidence therefore best supports a Novel classification.

None of the provided articles addresses Autism Spectrum Disorder in any way. The GAL3ST2 literature here concerns sulfotransferase glycan biology (3-O-sulfated galactose epitopes), mucin sulfation in intestinal goblet-like cells, antiviral glycan remodeling, allergic conjunctivitis susceptibility, and a proteome-wide Mendelian randomization implicating GAL3ST2 in Alzheimer's disease CSF biomarkers. The Alzheimer's MR study is a human genetic study but targets a distinct neurodegenerative phenotype, not autism or a recognized autism precursor. There is no expression, pathway, animal-model, or variant evidence linking GAL3ST2 to autism, so the co-mention is essentially absent rather than incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

No article reports FGF19 variants in autism patients, families, or cohorts; there is no human genetic association evidence, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded. The overwhelming majority of the retrieved literature concerns FGF19 as an endocrine FGF in bile acid/metabolic regulation (PMIDs 21813638, 30455427, 35682726, 26834701, 37260446) and as an oncogenic driver in hepatocellular carcinoma (PMIDs 25822088, 38228803, 31168847), which is incidental to Autism Spectrum Disorder. The only tenuous link is PMID 24648391, where FGF8/FGF19 signaling modulation directs medial versus caudal ganglionic eminence fate during human pluripotent stem cell–derived GABAergic interneuron specification, with autism mentioned as a disorder of interneuron/inhibitory circuit imbalance. This provides a weak, indirect biological/pathway rationale (in vitro human cells) that could support a Hypothesized rating, but autism is co-mentioned only as background motivation rather than tested. Consequently, points are concentrated on Novel with a substantial minority on Hypothesized.

Both provided articles concern HAUS1 in glioma biology (prognostic modeling and tumour microenvironment/immune infiltration), with no mention of Autism Spectrum Disorder, neurodevelopment, or human genetic variants linked to autism. No clinical studies in probands or families are presented, so Established and Existing cannot be supported. The only conceivable biological link (microtubule nucleation/cell cycle in neural cells) is not articulated in these abstracts, giving very weak support for Hypothesized. The evidence base here is essentially incidental co-mention, supporting a Novel classification.

None of the provided articles mention autism spectrum disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype. The literature on HACD3 (PTPLAD1) concerns very-long-chain fatty acid elongation, NSCLC progression, type 2 diabetes/MASLD metabolic networks, and cardiac chamber-specific gene expression in piglets. There are no human genetic association studies, no probands or families, and no mechanistic or animal-model data linking HACD3 to autism. Therefore the co-mentions are incidental and provide no logical basis for a gene–phenotype relationship, supporting a Novel classification with only a small allowance for indirect lipid-metabolism biology relevant to neurodevelopment.

Both provided articles concern CRISPR-Cas13 enzymes, where "HEPN1"/"HEPN-1" refers to a "Higher Eukaryotes and Prokaryotes Nucleotide-binding" domain of bacterial Cas13 proteins, not the human HEPN1 (hepatocellular carcinoma, downregulated 1) gene. These are homonym acronym hits and should be dismissed. Neither study involves humans, neurodevelopment, or Autism Spectrum Disorder, and no genetic variants in patients are reported. There is therefore no evidence—genetic, functional, or biological—linking HEPN1 to ASD in this literature set.

No article reports ICAM5 variants identified in autism probands or families; the human genetic studies present concern gastroschisis, breast cancer, varenicline-induced dreams, and Inuit population genetics, which are unrelated to ASD. The strongest ASD-relevant evidence is biological: ICAM5 is an FMRP target whose overexpression drives dendritic spine dysgenesis in Fmr1 KO mice, and knockdown rescues cognitive and anxiety-like phenotypes (PMID 31882402, 31680833) — a mechanism tied to Fragile X syndrome, the leading monogenic cause of ASD, but demonstrated in mouse/in vitro models, not human genetic association. Additional supporting biology includes ICAM5's role in dendritic targeting, synaptic plasticity, and enhanced LTP/sensorimotor gating in Tlcn knockout mice (PMIDs 15689548, 11135016). This constitutes strong pathway/animal-model plausibility without human variant evidence, so Hypothesized is the best fit.

None of the provided articles mention autism spectrum disorder, autistic features, or any neurodevelopmental/behavioral phenotype. The literature exclusively concerns IFT20's role in intraflagellar transport, ciliogenesis, Golgi trafficking, and resulting phenotypes in kidney (cystic disease), retina, bone/cartilage, sperm flagella, and cell migration, largely in mouse, Chlamydomonas, and in vitro models. Human variant reports cited (TRIP11, CEP78, DNHD1, CCDC146, TULP2) implicate other genes, with IFT20 only as an interacting partner, so they provide no human genetic evidence linking IFT20 to ASD. A residual "Hypothesized" allocation reflects only the general and indirect notion that primary cilia/ciliary signaling (Hedgehog, Wnt) participate in neurodevelopment, which is not demonstrated for IFT20 in any of these papers.

None of the provided articles report LAMB4 variants in autism spectrum disorder patients or cohorts; the human genetic findings concern diverticulitis, endometriosis, colorectal/gastric cancer, HNSCC, and MDS (PMIDs 28595269, 40868176, 23585368, 25257191, 36081907, 33667811), which are unrelated to ASD. The only neurobiologically relevant work shows that LAMB4 is required for human neural crest cell migration and peripheral sensory neuron development, with variants modifying severity of Familial Dysautonomia (PMID 39605577); this provides a plausible but indirect neurodevelopmental/ECM mechanism rather than any ASD-specific evidence. Familial dysautonomia and enteric nervous system innervation are not recognized ASD precursors or subtypes, so "Existing" is not supported. Thus the evidence base is largely incidental co-mention, with a modest case for a hypothesized neurodevelopmental link via laminin-mediated neural crest/neuronal migration.

None of the provided articles address autism spectrum disorder in any way. The available literature links LY6G5C to migraine target discovery via eQTL/GWAS integration (PMID 41097341), mouse male subfertility after CRISPR disruption (PMID 36428102), and differential methylation in pancreatic cancer (PMID 35030986). There are no human genetic variant studies, expression data, pathway links, or animal models connecting LY6G5C to autism or any recognized autism precursor/subtype. Therefore no evidence—direct or indirect—supports a gene–phenotype relationship, and the classification is Novel.

None of the provided articles mentions Autism Spectrum Disorder or reports any variant in L3MBTL3 in autistic probands or families, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The only human genetic association reported (rs13209574) concerns lean mass index in an elderly sarcopenia/frailty cohort (PMID 41015547), which is unrelated to ASD. The remaining literature is mechanistic and in vitro/mouse, showing L3MBTL3 as a methyl-lysine reader controlling proteolysis of SOX2, EZH2, and SWI/SNF subunits (SMARCC1/2), and acting as an RBPJ/Notch corepressor (PMIDs 30442713, 36335117, 38346162, 36477367) — pathways (chromatin remodeling, Notch, embryonic lethality in Lmbtl3-null mice) that are broadly relevant to neurodevelopment and could support a weak hypothesized link. Because this biological relevance is indirect and no ASD phenotype is measured, most probability falls on Novel with a substantial share on Hypothesized.

None of the provided articles report LARGE2 (GYLTL1B) variants in autism spectrum disorder patients; the literature is dominated by biochemical characterization of LARGE2 as a bifunctional xylosyl-/glucuronyltransferase acting on α-dystroglycan (PMIDs 15958417, 23135544, 23125099, 25138275, 15661757) and by dystroglycanopathy/muscular dystrophy contexts. The only human genetic report (PMID 23239541) is a 137-kb contiguous-gene deletion at 11p11.2 encompassing six genes (including GYLTL1B) in a child with developmental delay, hypotonia and neurobehavioral abnormalities—this cannot implicate LARGE2 specifically and does not describe ASD, so it does not support Existing or Established. Non-human data (zebrafish morphants, Large2−/− mice, a mouse lemur with a LARGE2 mutation and behavioral/motor/ocular pathology, PMIDs 18632251, 30486920) provide only indirect neurodevelopmental plausibility, which at best supports Hypothesized. Because the biological link to ASD is generic (CNS involvement in dystroglycanopathies) rather than ASD-specific, most weight falls between Novel and Hypothesized.

None of the provided articles addresses Autism Spectrum Disorder. The MFAP3L findings concern Lyme borreliosis–related monocyte metabolism/platelet degranulation (PMID 36001729), a gene-based association with anxiety disorder quantitative traits (PMID 25390645), and rare-variant aggregation in childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (PMID 41484610) — none is a recognized precursor, subtype, or mechanism of ASD. The anxiety GWAS gene-based signal is a human psychiatric association, which gives a very small allowance for a broader neuropsychiatric link, but it is not ASD and did not reach single-locus genome-wide significance. There are no probands, families, functional neurodevelopmental data, or animal models connecting MFAP3L to autism, so an Established rating is impossible and Novel is the best fit.

The single available article (PMID 30524470) describes a de novo ~500 kb 12q13.2-q13.3 deletion encompassing over 25 genes in a patient with Diamond-Blackfan anemia, Pierre Robin sequence and Klippel-Feil deformity; autism spectrum disorder is not mentioned at all. MYL6B is only listed incidentally among deleted genes with speculated roles in muscle function and bone development, and a multigenic contiguous deletion cannot implicate a single gene in any case. There is no genetic, expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence linking MYL6B to ASD in this literature set. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for hypothesized biological relevance given the gene's presence in a neurodevelopmentally relevant CNV region.

No article in this set reports autism spectrum disorder in individuals with MRPL49 variants. The two clinical reports of bi-allelic MRPL49 variants (PMIDs 39417135, 40043708) and the case report (PMID 40715997) describe combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency phenotypes—Perrault syndrome, sensorineural hearing loss, leukodystrophy, learning disability, microcephaly, retinal dystrophy, dystonia—but not ASD; learning disability/microcephaly are neurodevelopmental but not recognized ASD precursors specific enough to count as an ASD association. The remaining papers are reviews, expression surveys, yeast work, and unrelated bioinformatics comorbidity analyses (stroke/ESRD, Parkinson's), which are incidental co-mentions. A weak hypothesized rationale exists because mitoribosomal/OXPHOS dysfunction and mitochondrial disease are broadly discussed as neurodevelopmental risk mechanisms, and the gene causes CNS phenotypes, but this is indirect. Therefore the evidence best supports Novel, with meaningful weight on Hypothesized.

The single provided article (PMID 25366156) concerns NOL4 (not NOL4L, a distinct paralog) splicing variants interacting with Mlr1/Mlr2 transcription factors, using mouse brain cDNA libraries, yeast two-hybrid, GST pull-down, and Drosophila S2 cell luciferase assays. It contains no mention of Autism Spectrum Disorder, no human subjects, and no genetic variants in patients. There are therefore no PMIDs demonstrating causal variants in independent probands or families, precluding "Established" or "Existing." A small amount of weight is retained for "Hypothesized" because the gene family encodes brain-expressed transcriptional coregulators, a biologically plausible class for neurodevelopmental phenotypes, but the abstract makes no link to ASD, so "Novel" is the best fit for the evidence supplied.

None of the provided articles mention autism spectrum disorder at all; PCBD1 variants are consistently linked to transient neonatal hyperphenylalaninemia/primapterinuria, MODY-like early-onset diabetes, renal magnesium wasting, and cataract, with the PCBD1 form of BH4 deficiency generally described as benign. No human study reports ASD probands or families with PCBD1 variants, so Established and Existing are not supportable. The only conceivable link is indirect biology: PCBD1 participates in BH4 recycling, and BH4 deficiencies can cause central monoamine neurotransmitter deficiency and neurodevelopmental/neurological sequelae (PMIDs 33903016, 37818795, 36313470), a pathway sometimes invoked in ASD, which gives modest weight to Hypothesized. Otherwise, the co-mentions are incidental and the relationship appears Novel.

No article demonstrates NPTX1 point variants causing autism in patients; the human NPTX1 variant literature (PMIDs 34788392, 35285082, 35560436, 37479376, 40956878) concerns autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA50), not ASD, so Established is excluded. The only autism-specific human study (PMID 21254553) nominates NPTX1 as an in-silico candidate within multi-gene unbalanced chromosomal rearrangements, which by the stated rules cannot single out this gene and provides only weak, non-replicated support for Existing. Stronger support comes from biological plausibility: NPTX1 is released presynaptically downstream of astrocyte-secreted glypican 4/PTPRδ signaling to cluster AMPA receptors and drive excitatory synapse formation, a pathway explicitly linked to autism and schizophrenia (PMID 29024665), and it participates in glutamatergic/AMPA synaptic plasticity relevant to cognition (PMID 33328525). Remaining articles (MKRN E3 ligase biology, pentraxins in autoimmunity, CKD endothelium, SEGA/mTOR, cannabis use disorder) are unrelated to ASD. This profile best fits Hypothesized, with meaningful residual weight on Existing.

The only article directly connecting PHB2 to autism is a narrative review (PMID 37524128) that lists autism among many CNS conditions in which prohibitins are "prominently involved," reflecting expression/functional observations rather than any patient variant data; it does not report primary genetic findings. All other PHB2 papers concern mitophagy biology (PHB2 as an inner mitochondrial membrane mitophagy receptor, PINK1/PRKN pathways, ischemia, kidney injury, cardiac progenitors), which provides plausible neurobiological relevance (mitochondrial dysfunction is a recognized mechanism in ASD) but no ASD-specific genetic evidence. The Chinese CNV study (PMID 36750796) is a multigene copy-number survey that cannot single out PHB2, and other listed autism papers (CDKL5, SLC6A8 paralog, circadian, ABR animal model, conference abstracts) are unrelated to PHB2. No human study reports PHB2 sequence variants in ASD probands or families, so Established is essentially excluded and Existing is weakly supported at best; the biological plausibility places most weight on Hypothesized.

All "PLB" mentions in these articles are homonym acronyms, not the PLB1 (phospholipase B1) gene: the two autism papers (PMIDs 40392418, 40867131) use PLB for the natural compound plumbagin administered in a valproic acid rat model, and the remaining cardiac papers use PLB for phospholamban (PLN). The only article actually mentioning the PLB1 locus (PMID 30369316) reports a PPP1CB/PLB1 association with HDL cholesterol efflux capacity, a lipid trait unrelated to autism. There is therefore no genetic, expression, or mechanistic evidence connecting PLB1 to autism spectrum disorder in these sources, and no human proband or family data. The co-mentions are purely incidental acronym collisions, supporting a Novel classification.

None of the provided articles report autism spectrum disorder in association with PLOD3 variants; no proband, family, cohort, or association study links the gene to ASD, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The PLOD3-related literature centers on connective tissue disease (BCARD/Stickler-like syndrome), collagen glycosylation biology, cancer, and Parkinson's disease biomarkers. The only tenuous neuro-relevant signals are brain abnormalities (polymicrogyria, heterotopia, focal epilepsy) in one BCARD patient (PMID 40289369), cerebral small vessel disease from PLOD3 mutation (PMID 36203519), and brain phenotypes rescued in zebrafish plod3 mutants (PMID 41827019); these indicate CNS involvement broadly but are not ASD-specific and would at best support a weak hypothesized biological link. Accordingly, most probability mass falls on Novel, with a moderate allocation to Hypothesized based on these indirect neurodevelopmental/CNS findings.

No article in this set reports variants in PTH2 (TIP39) in individuals with autism spectrum disorder. Several papers concern PTRH2, a completely different gene causing IMNEPD (PMIDs 31057140, 27129381, 37239392, 35028776), and one is an unrelated bacterial/archaeal peptidyl-tRNA hydrolase "pth2" homonym (PMID 12475929); these must be dismissed. The only autism-related paper (PMID 26076356) concerns AKAP8/AKAP8L and TPTE/PTEN2 at 19p13.12, not PTH2. Remaining PTH2/PTH2R literature is endocrine, oncologic, zebrafish developmental, or neuroanatomical (PMIDs 19857544, 21880859), with the TIP39–PTH2R system implicated in affective behavior modulation in rodents — a weak, indirect biological rationale at best. Hence the relationship is essentially Novel, with only a small allowance for a hypothesized neuromodulatory link.

Nearly all retrieved articles concern the Arabidopsis DELLA protein RGL2 (RGA-LIKE2), a gibberellin signaling repressor, which is a homonym unrelated to the human RGL2 gene and must be dismissed (e.g., PMIDs 19500306, 19325888, 18162586, 16034591, 11826301). Only two papers address the human/mammalian RGL2: PMID 8939933 identifies RGL2 as a RalGDS-related candidate effector of Ras/Rap1 in vitro, and PMID 41554047 is a TWAS methods paper implicating RGL2 in type 1 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis — neither relates to Autism Spectrum Disorder. No human genetic variant study, expression study, animal model, or pathway argument connecting RGL2 to autism is present. Therefore there is no basis for Established or Existing, and only a negligible speculative basis (generic Ras signaling relevance to neurodevelopment) for Hypothesized.

The strongest human genetic evidence is the Autism Genome Project GWAS (PMID 20663923), where exploratory phenotypic-subtype analyses yielded strong signals within POU6F2, though not genome-wide significant in the primary analysis and not independently replicated. Supporting human data include differential expression of POU6F2 in single-nucleus cortical tissue from autism versus control cases and its co-occurrence with autism/schizophrenia-linked TFs in L4 glutamatergic neurons (PMID 40520596), and an OCD epigenetic study reporting a differentially methylated region in POU6F2, citing prior schizophrenia/autism links as background (PMID 41371113) — the latter is a citation rather than primary evidence. No paper reports pathogenic POU6F2 variants in autism probands or families; the human variant studies concern hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (PMID 37600690) and Wilms tumor (PMID 15459955), with other work in rats, zebrafish, mice, and cattle. This profile fits "Existing" (limited, non-definitive human association) with meaningful residual probability for "Hypothesized" if the GWAS subtype signal is discounted as exploratory.

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype. The SIGLEC15 literature here is exclusively about osteoclast biology/bone remodeling (PMIDs 21586272, 22451653, 23238125, 23677868, 25460183, 26027508, 38849345), Siglec family evolution/immunology (35989204, 32152949), DAP12-associated inflammatory disease (42089995), and one human exome-wide association with tuberculosis susceptibility (30898644). There are no human genetic variant data, expression findings, or mechanistic pathways linking SIGLEC15 to autism. Consequently, the relationship is best described as Novel, with only a negligible allowance for indirect neuroimmune/DAP12–microglia reasoning that could support a speculative hypothesis.

None of the provided articles reports any genetic variant, association study, or clinical cohort linking SGSM1 to Autism Spectrum Disorder; autism is not mentioned at all. The only biologically relevant paper (PMID 17509819) shows SGSM1 is predominantly expressed in brain neurons and modulates RAP/RAB small G protein signaling and vesicular trafficking, which is a pathway class loosely relevant to neurodevelopmental disorders, giving weak plausibility for a "Hypothesized" rating. The remaining papers concern unrelated phenotypes (age-related macular degeneration family-based rare-variant suggestive signal, congenital heart disease allele-specific expression, canine obesity structural variants, ALS/depression bioinformatics hub genes, mouse germline stem cells), and are incidental co-mentions with no autism relevance. There are no human ASD probands or families implicating SGSM1, so Established and Existing are effectively unsupported.

No article in this set reports PRDM16 point/sequence variants segregating with autism in independent probands or families, so Established is untenable. The strongest human evidence is the sperm epigenome-wide study (PMID 41474634), which maps age-related differentially methylated CpGs to imprinted genes including PRDM16 and explicitly links them to ASD risk — a credible but indirect and limited human association. Additional human support is only indirect: PRDM16 lies within the 1p36 deletion region (PMIDs 26345236, 41327254) associated with neurodevelopmental phenotypes, but a multigene CNV cannot single out PRDM16, and the ASD microarray study (PMID 42286492) does not implicate PRDM16 specifically. Remaining papers concern adipose browning, kidney injury, cardiomyopathy, migraine and leukemia (PMIDs 34915728, 39549609, 35075301, 34588893), which are irrelevant or at best offer generic biological plausibility, supporting a substantial Hypothesized weighting and some residual probability of Novel.
