Multiple independent human studies report gene-specific (not merely multigene CNV) variants in PTCHD1 in ASD probands: Noor et al. (PMID 20844286) identified seven maternally inherited missense changes in eight male ASD probands plus exon-1/whole-gene deletions in unrelated families; Chaudhry et al. (PMID 25131214) described 23 individuals with PTCHD1 deletions or truncating (loss-of-function) mutations, >40% with ASD or ASD-like behaviour; Halewa et al. (PMID 33856728) reported 13 missense variants in males with ID/ASD with functional evidence of mislocalization; Torrico et al. (PMID 25782667) added rare promoter and common-variant association in ASD cohorts. These are independent probands/families with point mutations, satisfying the requirement for replicated causal evidence in humans, and further support comes from CRISPR/iPSC modeling of a patient variant (PMID 38007613) and clinical panel data (PMID 40019509). Some residual uncertainty remains because the core phenotype is X-linked intellectual disability with variable autistic features, and several implicated deletions also involve PTCHD1-AS/DDX53, which is why a portion of probability is kept on "Existing".

None of the provided articles reports autism spectrum disorder as an outcome of SKOR2 variation. Human genetic evidence exists for biallelic SKOR2 variants causing cerebellar hypoplasia, microcephaly, ataxia, developmental/speech delay and intellectual disability (PMIDs 41821366, 40890458), a neurodevelopmental phenotype spectrum that overlaps with, but is not explicitly, ASD; this partial overlap justifies some weight for "Existing." The strongest support is biological/mechanistic: SKOR2/Corl2 governs Purkinje cell differentiation and TGF-β/Smad signalling (PMIDs 24491816, 35030229), and Drosophila CORL mutants show movement and behavioural plasticity phenotypes (PMID 32161085) — cerebellar Purkinje cell development being a pathway repeatedly implicated in autism. No study demonstrates ASD-specific probands or replication, so "Established" is untenable, and the balance falls to "Hypothesized."

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder, autism-related phenotypes, or any neurodevelopmental genetic association with TLCD1. The literature exclusively concerns TLCD1 as a lipid acyltransferase regulating phosphatidylethanolamine composition (PMIDs 39970228, 36241646, 40266577) and as a cancer biomarker (PMIDs 38559424, 42218213), with no human genetic variant studies in autism probands or families. The only tangential neurological link is the related family member CLN8 in Batten disease, which concerns a different gene and a different (neurodegenerative) phenotype, giving at most a weak biological rationale via membrane lipid homeostasis in the brain. Therefore no evidence supports Established or Existing, and only a small allowance is made for a speculative biological/pathway hypothesis.

No article in this list reports SLF1 variants in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder. The only human genetic finding is a single de novo SLF1 variant in one female with Aicardi Syndrome (PMID 37628618), a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder; that same paper shows Slf1 expression in developing mouse cortex, which supports a plausible biological (neurodevelopmental) link rather than an ASD-specific association. Remaining papers concern the yeast Slf1p La-motif RNA-binding protein (PMIDs 10564276, 22271760), fish methylation (PMID 35585152), and RAD18–SLF1–SMC5/6 genome-stability biology (PMIDs 38884202, 36333305), which are either homonymous or mechanistically generic and not ASD-relevant. Thus the evidence best fits Hypothesized (single-patient human NDD variant plus cortical expression data), with some weight on Existing if Aicardi-type NDD is accepted as an ASD-related phenotype, and residual weight on Novel given the absence of any autism-specific data.

Neither provided article addresses Autism Spectrum Disorder. One paper concerns TBC1D25 in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (lipid accumulation and inflammation, largely mouse/in vitro), and the other reports an X-linked missense variant causing oligozoospermia/male infertility in a single family — a phenotype unrelated to autism. There is no genetic, expression, neurodevelopmental, or pathway-level evidence linking TBC1D25 to autism in these abstracts. A minor allowance is made for the gene's X-linked location and autophagy function, which could theoretically be neurodevelopmentally relevant, but this is not asserted in any provided literature.

None of the provided articles mention autism spectrum disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype linked to TPCN2. The human genetic evidence for TPCN2 concerns pigmentation phenotypes (albinism, hypopigmentation, blond hair, melanoma risk) via gain-of-function variants such as p.R210C, and disease links are otherwise to Parkinson's disease, lysosomal storage/trafficking, and infection. Some biological plausibility exists only indirectly, since endolysosomal Ca2+ signaling and lysosomal trafficking dysfunction are broadly implicated in neuronal function and neurodegeneration, but no data connect TPC2 to autism pathophysiology or autism-associated variants. Therefore the relationship is essentially unsupported (Novel), with a small allowance for a generic mechanistic/hypothesized argument.

Most retrieved articles containing "SPR" are homonyms and must be dismissed: the C. elegans chromatin genes spr-1/spr-5 (PMIDs 36655746, 26691751, 40991443), the Sprouty-related (SPR) domain of SPRED1 (39510187), and surface plasmon resonance "SPR" in the neuropeptide paper (42570625). The genuine sepiapterin reductase literature (10727395, 33903016, 26131547, 21677200, 34908184, 20590807) establishes SPR variants as a cause of BH4 deficiency/dopa-responsive dystonia with monoamine neurotransmitter deficiency, developmental delay and cognitive/behavioral features, and one review speculatively lists autism among conditions possibly related to restricted BH4 cofactor availability. However, no article here reports ASD-diagnosed probands or families with SPR variants, and no genetic association study of SPR in autism cohorts is present. The plausible biological link (serotonin/dopamine biosynthesis, neurodevelopmental phenotypes) supports "Hypothesized," with some probability for "Existing" given that SPR deficiency phenotypes include neurodevelopmental impairment that can overlap ASD features. "Established" is untenable because not even one primary study of SPR variants in ASD patients is cited.

The only provided article (PMID 25241935) concerns TRIM58 as an E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades dynein during terminal erythropoiesis, with relevance to erythrocyte traits, not neurodevelopment. No study in the list reports TRIM58 variants in individuals with autism spectrum disorder, nor any expression, pathway, or animal-model link to ASD. There is therefore no human genetic evidence supporting Established or Existing, and no biologically relevant mechanism proposed for ASD to support Hypothesized (a small residual allowance is given because dynein/microtubule regulation is broadly relevant to neuronal biology). The evidence base is essentially absent, so Novel is by far the most appropriate category.

None of the provided articles examine autism spectrum disorder; the literature concerns migraine (PMIDs 30258394, 40910422, 41833043), stroke (27796860), blood pressure methylation (29198723), pancreatic β-cell apoptosis (27247127), endometriosis (42141251), and cancer/oligodendrocyte biology (28408487). No human genetic study reports TSPAN2 variants in autism probands or families, ruling out Established and Existing. A weak biological rationale could be argued from TSPAN2's role in oligodendrocyte differentiation/myelination and microglial neuroinflammatory signaling (28408487, 31823250), processes broadly implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, which justifies a modest Hypothesized allocation. However, these are indirect and not autism-specific, so the co-mentions are essentially incidental and Novel is most likely.

No articles were provided linking ZNF653 to Autism Spectrum Disorder, so there is no evidence of variants in patients, no functional or expression data, and no pathway or animal model support. Without any literature, the relationship cannot be considered established or existing, and there is no biological rationale documented to support a hypothesized link. The default classification is therefore Novel, with small residual probability reflecting the possibility that relevant literature exists but was not supplied (e.g., ZNF653 appearing in large-scale neurodevelopmental sequencing datasets).

No articles were provided, so there is no literature evidence linking ZNF710 to Autism Spectrum Disorder. Without any citations demonstrating variants in probands or families, Established and Existing cannot be supported. ZNF710 is a zinc-finger transcription factor that could plausibly have neurodevelopmental relevance, so a small probability is retained for Hypothesized based on generic biology. The absence of any supporting literature makes Novel the most probable category.

None of the provided articles reports VEPH1 variants in autism spectrum disorder probands or families, so Established is excluded. The closest human genetic evidence is a gene-based association of VEPH1 with developmental dyslexia (PMID 33057169), a different neurodevelopmental phenotype with shared polygenic overlap with psychiatric traits, but not a recognized precursor or subtype of ASD; this only weakly supports "Existing". Biologically, VEPH1 is expressed in the ventricular zone, its Drosophila ortholog melted produces a severe neural phenotype, and it modulates TOR/mTORC1, FoxO, Hippo, TGFβ and AKT signaling (PMIDs 31500637, 32610114) — pathways strongly implicated in ASD — which provides a plausible mechanistic rationale supporting "Hypothesized". The remaining papers concern cancer and vascular smooth muscle biology and are irrelevant to ASD, leaving meaningful probability for "Novel".

Two independent human probands with biallelic ACY1 variants and confirmed enzyme deficiency have been reported with autistic phenotypes: PMID 20480396 (homozygous c.1057C>T, p.Arg353Cys, patient diagnosed with autistic syndrome) and PMID 29653693 (compound heterozygous ACY1 mutations, mild intellectual disability with autistic traits and 4-year follow-up); PMID 24117009 also lists autistic features within the ACY1 deficiency spectrum. However, the literature repeatedly emphasizes that ACY1 deficiency's clinical significance is uncertain and may represent a biochemical variant rather than a causal disease (PMIDs 16465618, 16274666), and several reported patients lack autistic features (PMID 24997716, 26686503, 37523070), with the phenotype being highly variable and non-specific. This inconsistent, small-N, non-replicated genotype–phenotype correlation supports a credible but limited association rather than an established causal relationship. Additional papers (metabolomic GWAS, proteomics, SON splicing) mention ACY1 only incidentally to other traits and do not add ASD-specific evidence.
